payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the image into pencil drawing
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Are the scene's principal shapes and edges represented with visibly pencil-drawn contour linework?
node.criteria: Pass if visibly drawn, pencil-like strokes describe the principal objects and internal boundaries across the scene. Require identifiable graphite-like articulation, such as sketch-like stroke segments, repeated tracing or stroke-level variation in line weight, distinguishable from the source's photographic edges. Darker or softer photographic boundaries, sharpening halos, muted colors and uniform grain alone do not satisfy this condition. Fail if principal contours remain photographic or merely contrast-enhanced without convincing drawn stroke structure. Use unknown only when the available visual evidence cannot establish the contour style.
node.binding: Compare the supplied SOURCE and EDITED images against the requested pencil-drawing transformation. Inspect corresponding contours of the plate, food, fork, glass and pitcher, distinguishing pencil-like drawn linework in the edit from boundaries already present in the source. Evaluate contour rendering independently of interior shading.

node_traces.evidence: The edit is muted and grainy, but the plate, food, fork, glass, and pitcher boundaries remain smooth photographic edges. There are no convincing pencil-like stroke segments, repeated tracing, or stroke-level line-weight variation distinguishing the contours from the source.

d1_shading: The node’s visual evidence supports a genuine partial transformation: the edit is markedly desaturated and softened, with a grainy, sketch-like treatment and some altered contours, while much of the original photographic form and surface rendering remains. The current criterion makes pervasive pencil-style shading the sole pass condition, so it can correctly flag incomplete fulfillment but cannot distinguish “some requested change progressed” from “no requested change.” Preserve the strict completion test; add an explicit progress assessment that compares SOURCE with EDITED and recognizes visible pencil-like or tonal-style changes as partial progress even when photographic gradients, reflections, or textures remain. Keep unrelated changes from counting, and reserve unknown for inadequate visual evidence. The trace is valid and has no transport, schema, or dependency failure; the mismatch is criterion/label granularity, not evidence that the edit is complete.
